title: An empirical study of race times in recreational endurance runners
journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
population: Recreational endurance runners recruited by internet survey; cohort split 2:1 into training and validation sets
findings: Sex, age, BMI and race training were associated with mean race velocity for all race distances; the male-female velocity difference decreased with increasing distance.
Tempo runs were more strongly associated with velocity for shorter distances; typical weekly training mileage and interval training had similar associations with velocity at all distances.
The Riegel formula was well calibrated for races up to a half marathon but dramatically underestimated marathon time, giving times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners.
Mean squared error for marathon time was 381 for Riegel versus 228 for a model based on one prior race and 208 for a model based on two prior races (units not stated in the abstract).
Sex, age, BMI and race training were associated with mean race velocity at all distances; the male-female velocity difference shrank with distance.
Tempo runs were more strongly associated with velocity for shorter distances; typical weekly mileage and interval training had similar associations for all distances.
Riegel's formula was well calibrated to the half-marathon but dramatically underestimated marathon time, giving times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners.
Marathon prediction mean squared error: 381 (Riegel) vs 228 (one prior race model) and 208 (two prior races).
limitations: Self-reported survey data from a self-selected internet sample; internal 2:1 split only, no external cohort; the abstract does not give model coefficients, which anchor race distance was used in the Riegel comparison, the MSE units, or whether trail/ultra distances were covered.
implications: Do not use a single-race Riegel extrapolation to the marathon without a correction and an optimistic-bias flag; Riegel is acceptable up to the half marathon.
Where two prior race results exist, prefer a model that uses both (plus sex, age, BMI, weekly mileage) over single-race Riegel; MSE fell from 381 to 208.

Use weekly mileage and the share of tempo/interval work as covariates, with tempo weighted more for races up to the half marathon. If MSE is in min^2 (not confirmed), RMSE is about 19.5 min for Riegel versus 14.4 min with two races.
Do not extrapolate shorter-race results to the marathon with the plain Riegel exponent; use a corrected model using one or two prior races and weekly mileage.
Include weekly mileage, sex, age and BMI as inputs to goal-time prediction.
